<li><strong>Predicted indications (10)</strong>:<ul>

<li>Esophageal varices without bleeding | 97.56% | L5 | Hold | Theoretical: portal hypertension drives VEGF-mediated collateral angiogenesis; no preclinical validation (99.0%)</li>
<li>Esophageal varices with bleeding | 97.56% | L5 | Hold | Same as above; acute hemorrhage adds hemostatic safety concern (99.0%)</li>
<li>Varicose disease | 96.95% | L5 | Hold | VEGF linked to venous wall remodeling, but core pathology is mechanical; indirect link (99.0%)</li>
<li>Urethral calculus | 95.97% | L5 | Hold | No credible mechanistic link to VEGF; assessed as graph artifact (99.0%)</li>
<li>Adenosine deaminase deficiency | 95.76% | L5 | Hold | No mechanistic link; assessed as knowledge-graph false positive (99.0%)</li>
<li>Hemorrhagic disease of newborn | 95.56% | L5 | Hold | Pathology is vitamin K-dependent; anti-VEGF may worsen bleeding tendency — safety concern (99.0%)</li>
<li>Ectomesenchymoma | 94.52% | L5 | Research Question | Rare malignancy; VEGF overexpression in soft tissue tumors plausible; class-extension hypothesis (99.0%)</li>
<li>Malignant cutaneous granular cell skin tumor | 94.51% | L5 | Hold | Schwann cell origin; VEGF as driver is weakly supported (99.0%)</li>
<li>Middle ear neuroendocrine tumor | 94.42% | L5 | Research Question | NETs are typically hypervascular; anti-angiogenic class-extension hypothesis reasonable (99.0%)</li>
